title: TTL
subtitle: Time-To-Live expiration mechanics, active vs passive expiry in Redis, and TTL jitter to prevent synchronized thundering herds.
keyTakeaways: Every cached key requires an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) to bound data staleness and prevent abandoned keys from consuming RAM indefinitely.
Fixed TTLs cause synchronized mass expirations (Cache Avalanches); applying random jitter distributes expirations smoothly over time.
Caches clean expired keys using a mix of passive checks during read access and periodic active probabilistic sampling in the background.

sections.heading: Passive vs Active Expiration Mechanics
sections.body: An in-memory store cannot spin up 50 million OS timers for 50 million cached keys without melting its CPU. Redis balances memory reclamation against CPU cycles by splitting expiration into two distinct mechanisms.
bullets: Passive (Lazy) Expiration: Whenever a client runs `GET key`, the engine checks the key's timestamp. If expired, it removes the entry on the spot and returns `nil`. The limitation is that unread keys would linger in RAM forever without a cleanup loop.

Active Probabilistic Sampling: Ten times a second, the server samples 20 keys with TTLs at random, deletes the expired ones, and repeats immediately if more than 25% were dead. This prevents memory bloat while capping CPU usage to single-digit percentages.

Dual Expiration (Soft TTL vs Hard TTL): Store a business timestamp inside the payload alongside a longer Redis TTL. When a reader sees the soft TTL expired, it serves the cached payload immediately while queuing an asynchronous background refresh. Users see 0ms tail latency.

codeSnippet.title: Jittered TTL & Soft-TTL (Stale-While-Revalidate) Pattern

sections.heading: Defending Against the Cache Avalanche
sections.body: Cache Avalanches usually follow large deployments, daily cron syncs, or failover events where thousands of keys are written simultaneously. Without variance in the expiration calculation, they all expire at the same tick, sending an unbuffered traffic spike to the database.
bullets: Mandatory TTL Jitter: Add a random variance (`ttl = base_ttl + rand(0, jitter_range)`) to every write. A 3600-second base TTL with 10% jitter spreads expirations across a 360-second window, turning a cliff into a gentle slope.

Asynchronous Deallocation (`lazyfree-lazy-expire`): Expiring millions of large collection keys simultaneously can tie up Redis's main thread during active sampling. Setting `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` shifts memory free calls to background IO threads.
Tiered Expiration Windows: Classify cache keys by update volatility: static configurations (24h+), user sessions (1h), and rapidly changing counters (10–30s).

tradeOffs.pros: Keeps cache staleness tightly bounded without needing complex CDC or pub/sub invalidation pipelines.
tradeOffs.cons: Reduces cache hit ratio for tail records and generates steady background database read load.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Rapidly shifting dashboards, live public leaderboards, and aggregate counters.

tradeOffs.option: Long TTL with Soft Expiry & Invalidation
tradeOffs.pros: Maximizes cache hit ratio (>99%) and guarantees near-zero p99 read latency.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires operational maintenance of asynchronous refresh workers and invalidation queues.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Product catalogs, customer profile summaries, and merchant directory listings.

interviewTip: Highlighting TTL jitter alongside a Soft/Hard TTL split (Stale-While-Revalidate) shows you design for catastrophic edge cases like database thrashing rather than assuming happy-path traffic.
